newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand business weeklies - Nov 29.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand business weeklies - Nov 29.

text.p: A troubled Maori trust which has been at the centre of accountability concerns is threatened by a new tax treatment that could eat up millions of dollars worth of its income. The Crown Forestry Rental Trust, chaired by Sir Graham Latimer, may also have to pay as much as $12 million in back taxes.

The trust receives land rentals from operators with cutting rights over Crown-owned forestry land. It invests the rentals and uses the income to fund Maori claims over the land and is worried the loss of million of dollars worth of revenue to the IRD will substantially reduce its ability to assist claimants.

In the past there has been controversy over the level of fees and expenses paid to trustees. The trust has also been attacked from within Maoridom, with various tribes not knowing whether trust money was being fairly dispensed. Page 1.

The mystery financier involved in Auckland's controversial Britomart downtown redevelopment project was identified on Thursday as an exotic mixture of individuals and companies from Australia to Arabia. Page 1.

Accounting firm Coopers and Lybrand will have to pay tax on massive "inducement payments" its partners received for moving into new Auckland premises in 1991. The High Court has ruled that the lump-sum payments, from developers and building owners to the practice to persuade it to shift to a new tower in Albert Street, are assessable income. Page 1.

"Ditch your office" is one of Kevin Roberts' rules -- and now he is doing just that. The flamboyant chief operating officer of Lion Nathan is giving up his executive role -- although he will remain on the Lion Nathan board as a non-executive director from next February. The investment community has mixed views on whether Roberts' departure signals failure of the strategies he implemented during his eight years with the company. Page 3.

A U.S. company suing the Dairy Board has claimed the board is dragging its heels in the case to stop "smoking gun" documents from reaching the public domain. The board is defending allegations of fraud and breach of U.S. antitrust laws in a case which also threatens the U.S. operations of the Kiwifruit Marketing Board and the Apple and Pear Marketing Board. Page 8.

Telecom's Xtra Internet service faces legal action for allegedly publishing other services' information on its Web site. Three other sites face similar accusations. The disputes are this country's first major battles over copyright on the Internet and have raised questions over whether the current law is adequate. Page 12.

Only a month after our first MMP election, a rising number of New Zealanders said they disliked the outcome. While 39 percent were recorded in the latest NBR-Consultus poll as being happy with the result, 36 percent were unhappy -- up 10 percent on the number who said they disliked it just after the election. Page 14.

After nearly a week of market speculation, Sir Ron Brierley's Guiness Peat Group on Thursday revealed it had taken a stake in brewer DB Group. Tony Gibbs, a director of GPG (NZ) Ltd, confirmed his company had, over "several weeks", been buying shares. When asked for numbers, Gibbs said "many". The Independent understands GPG holds somewhere between three percent and four percent of DB, after beginning its buying spree in mid-October when the prices was around 85 cents. DB closed on Thursday at 97 cents. Page 1.

Clear Communications has launched yet another High Court action against Telecom, claiming its rival is abusing a monopoly position to keep competitors out of the market. With Clear's battle over Telecom's expansion into pay televison due to resume in the Wellington High Court on Monday, the company now has two actions against Telecom running simultaneously. Page 1.

Fresh data from the Forestry Ministry show why investors should be wary of forestry promoters promising astronomical returns based on projected future log price increases. The ministry's just-published analysis concludes log price movements in recent years have been only marginal in New Zealand dollar terms, have increased slightly in United States dollar terms, and have decreased in Japanese yen. These conclusions are in marked contrast to the claims of many forestry partnership promoters that log prices have increased in real terms by four percent per annum between 1910 and 1993, and future real price increases of that magnitude are realistic. Page 1.

An A$34.5 million public float in New Zealand and Australia may be a means of raising investment capital for Auckland's controversial $1.5 billion Britomart project. Britomart middleman Jihong Lu has revealed a consortium of international investors will provide A$80 million towards the project and a further A$34.5 million may be raised through a small group of investors or a public float. Page 2.

NZ First is preparing to tackle the crucial task of selling its coalition decision to its supporters, which opinion polls show are split on whether the party should go with National or Labour. NZ First is trying to limit potential for the decision to split the party -- already suffering from infighting -- by having it made jointly by MPs and the entire ruling council. Page 4.

Fletcher Homes, when agreeing to mediate with 15 of the 500 disgruntled homebuyers involved in the well-publicised "over-valuation" cases, maintained the fault lay in bogus specifications conjured up by its own staff. It was not, as alleged, inflated valuations, the company says. Page 4.

Lion Nathan chief operating officer Kevin Roberts is parting company with his employers. News on Thursday of the high profile executive's departure caught the brewing industry by surprise. Described by one analyst as a "dynamic executive and dedicated to the company", Roberts has overseen eight years of massive restructuring of Lion Nathan. Page 8.
